passages.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
paragraphs: In summer, the leaves on many trees are green. But in autumn, those same leaves can turn yellow, orange, or bright red. Where does all that color come from?

Leaves are green because of a substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll helps a tree make food from sunlight. All summer long, leaves are full of it, and the green is so strong that it hides every other color.
Leaves also contain yellow and orange colors the whole time. We just cannot see them in summer because the green chlorophyll covers them up.

As autumn arrives, the days grow shorter and the air turns cooler. The tree senses these changes and slowly stops making chlorophyll. As the green fades away, the yellows and oranges that were hidden all along finally show through.
Some trees even add a color that was not there before. In the fall, they make a new substance that turns their leaves deep red and purple.
Before winter, the leaves dry out and fall to the ground. The tree rests through the cold months and grows fresh green leaves again in spring, starting the cycle over.

passages.title: The Mixed-Up Lunchbox
paragraphs: When Ava opened her lunchbox at noon, she froze. Inside was a thick turkey sandwich, a chocolate brownie, and a little bag of strawberries. None of it was hers.

Her own lunch was plain: a cheese sandwich and an apple. Somehow, in the rush that morning, she had grabbed a lunchbox that looked just like hers off the kitchen counter — her older cousin Mateo’s lunchbox.
The brownie looked amazing. Ava’s stomach growled. No one would ever know, she thought.
But she pictured Mateo opening her plain little lunch, hungry after a long morning, and the brownie did not look quite so good anymore.
Ava closed the lunchbox and carried it to the office. “I think my cousin and I swapped lunches by accident,” she said. “Can you help me get his back to him?”
That afternoon, Mateo found her in the hall. “Thanks,” he said, and handed her half the brownie anyway. It tasted even better than she had imagined.

passages.title: The Bird That Never Stops Traveling
paragraphs: Twice a year, a small white seabird called the Arctic tern makes one of the most amazing journeys on Earth. It flies from the top of the world to the bottom and back again.

Arctic terns spend the northern summer near the Arctic, where they build nests and raise their chicks. When summer ends in the north, they do not simply fly a little south for the winter, the way many birds do.
Instead, they keep going — all the way to Antarctica, at the other end of the planet. There they find a second summer. Then, months later, they turn around and fly all the way back.

This round trip can cover tens of thousands of miles each year, making it the longest migration of any animal in the world. Over a lifetime, a single Arctic tern may fly far enough to reach the moon and back several times.
By chasing summer at both ends of the Earth, the Arctic tern sees more daylight in a year than almost any other creature. Its whole life is shaped by one incredible habit: it never stops traveling.

passages.title: The Tryout
paragraphs: Dev had wanted to make the school soccer team for as long as he could remember. At the first tryout, he ran hard, but when the coach read the list, his name was not on it.
He walked home slowly, his cleats slung over his shoulder. “Maybe I’m just not good enough,” he muttered.
His grandmother was on the porch. She listened, then said, “Not good enough yet. There is a big difference between ‘not good’ and ‘not yet.’”

The next morning, Dev started practicing in the empty lot behind his building. He dribbled around cans, kicked at a chalk goal on the wall, and ran until his legs burned. He did this every day for a year.
When tryouts came again, Dev moved differently — quicker, surer, his feet remembering a thousand hours of practice. This time, the coach called his name.
Walking home, Dev thought about the boy who had muttered “not good enough” a year ago. He smiled. His grandmother had been right. It had only ever been “not yet.”

passages.title: The Great Wall of China
paragraphs: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous structures ever built. Stretching across northern China, it winds over mountains and through deserts for thousands of miles.
The wall was not built all at once. Over many centuries, different rulers added to it and repaired it. Workers used stone, brick, and packed earth, often carrying materials up steep slopes by hand.

Why build something so enormous? The main purpose was defense. Northern China was often raided by armies on horseback, and the wall was meant to slow invaders down and give guards time to send warnings using smoke and fire signals.
The wall did more than block enemies. Gates along it controlled trade and travel, and soldiers stationed in towers kept watch over the land for miles around.

People sometimes claim you can see the Great Wall from space with the naked eye. This is not true. Although the wall is very long, it is narrow, and astronauts have said it is no easier to spot than many other human-made things.
Today the Great Wall is no longer needed for defense. Millions of people visit it each year to walk along the stones and imagine the workers and soldiers who once depended on it.

passages.title: The Treehouse Rule
paragraphs: Jojo and her two best friends, Sam and Priya, had built the treehouse together all summer, hauling boards and pounding nails until their arms ached.
Now that it was finished, a problem appeared. Sam wanted it to be a reading library. Priya wanted a spy headquarters. Jojo wanted an art studio. Each of them was sure their own idea was best.
For two days they argued, and nobody used the treehouse at all. It sat empty — the very thing they had worked so hard for going to waste.
On the third day, Jojo climbed up alone and looked around. There was a shelf, a quiet corner, and a wide flat wall. An idea came to her.
“What if,” she told the others, “the shelf is Sam’s library, the corner is Priya’s spy base, and the wall is my art space? It can be all three.”
Sam blinked. Priya grinned. By that afternoon the treehouse held books, a spyglass, and a half-finished painting, and the three of them were finally, happily, inside it together.

passages.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
paragraphs: If you have ever swallowed a mouthful of seawater, you know the ocean is salty. But rivers and rain are not salty, so where does all the salt come from?
The answer begins on land. As rain falls and rivers flow, the water moves over rocks and soil. Slowly, it dissolves tiny amounts of minerals, including salt, and carries them along.
Rivers carry this mineral-filled water to the sea. By itself, the amount of salt in any one river is far too small to taste. But rivers have been pouring into the ocean for millions of years.
Here is the key: when ocean water evaporates and rises into the air to form clouds, the salt is left behind. The water leaves, but the salt stays in the sea.
Over an enormous stretch of time, that salt has built up. Each year rivers add a little more, and each year evaporation leaves it behind, so the ocean stays salty while rivers do not.

passages.title: The Lemonade Stand
paragraphs: Carlos had planned his lemonade stand for a week. He made a bright sign, squeezed two pitchers of lemonade, and set up his table on the corner Saturday morning.
By ten o’clock, the sky turned gray. By ten-thirty, rain was pouring down, and Carlos dragged his soggy sign under the porch roof. Not one cup had sold.
He wanted to give up. But as he sat watching the rain, he noticed something: the mail carrier hurrying by, the neighbors dashing from their cars — everyone cold and wet.
Carlos went inside, and instead of pouring out his lemonade, he heated it on the stove with a little honey and cinnamon. He made a new sign in thick marker: HOT LEMONADE — 50 CENTS. WARM UP HERE.

He set up just inside the open garage, out of the rain. The mail carrier stopped first, then a jogger, then two neighbors. The warm cups disappeared faster than the cold ones ever would have on a sunny day.
That night Carlos counted his coins — more than he had hoped for. He realized the rain had not ruined his plan. It had only asked him to change it.

passages.title: How a Vaccine Teaches the Body to Fight
paragraphs: Your body has a built-in defense system called the immune system. When a harmful germ enters your body, the immune system learns to recognize it and builds special weapons, called antibodies, to destroy it. The trouble is that learning takes time, and during that time you can get sick.
A vaccine is a clever way to give the immune system a head start. It works by introducing a harmless version, or a tiny piece, of a germ — something that cannot actually make you sick.
When the immune system meets this harmless sample, it reacts as if it were facing the real germ. It studies the invader and produces antibodies designed to fight that exact germ.
The most important part comes next. After the threat is gone, the immune system keeps a kind of memory of it. Special memory cells remember how to make those antibodies.
Later, if the real germ ever shows up, the body does not have to start from scratch. The memory cells spring into action and defeat the germ so quickly that you may never feel sick at all.
This is why vaccines are so powerful. They let your body practice fighting a dangerous germ safely, before it ever has the chance to do real harm.

passages.title: The Photograph
paragraphs: In the shoebox of old pictures, Nadia found one she had never seen: a girl about her own age, laughing on a bicycle, frozen forever in black and white.
“Who is that?” she asked. Her grandfather looked over her shoulder and went quiet for a moment. “That,” he said softly, “is your great-grandmother. She was twelve there. Same age as you.”

Nadia stared. She had only ever known her great-grandmother as a name on a wall, an old woman in a few faded portraits. It had never occurred to her that this person had once been twelve, with scraped knees and a bicycle and a laugh caught mid-flight.
“What was she like?” Nadia asked. Her grandfather smiled. “Fearless. She rode that bike down the steepest hill in the village just to feel the wind. She would have liked you.”

Nadia held the photo carefully, as if it might fly away. The girl in the picture was not a stranger, and not quite the great-grandmother she had imagined. She was something new: a whole person, with a whole life, smiling at Nadia across a hundred years.

passages.title: Why the Sky Is Blue
paragraphs: On a clear day, the sky overhead is a deep, even blue. It is such a familiar sight that few people stop to ask why. The answer lies in the sunlight itself.

Sunlight may look white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave, and the colors have different wavelengths. Blue light travels in short waves, while red light travels in longer ones.
As sunlight enters the air, it crashes into the countless tiny molecules of gas that make up our atmosphere. These molecules scatter the light, bouncing it off in every direction.

Here is the key: the short waves of blue light scatter much more easily than the long waves of red light. So blue light gets thrown across the whole sky, reaching your eyes from every direction. That scattered blue is the color you see.

The same idea explains a sunset. When the sun sits low, its light must pass through much more air to reach you. Along that long path, the blue light is scattered away before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges to color the evening sky.

passages.title: The Trade
paragraphs: Eli had wanted Marcus’s knife for months — a folding camp knife with a smooth wooden handle, the kind that made you feel ready for any adventure. So when Marcus offered to trade it for Eli’s old fishing reel, Eli said yes before he could think twice.

The reel had been his grandfather’s. It was scratched and a little stiff, nothing special to look at. But Grandpa had taught Eli to cast with it on the dock, their feet dangling over the green water, summer after summer.
For a week, Eli carried the knife everywhere. He opened and closed it a hundred times. It was exactly as cool as he had imagined.

But one evening, sitting on the dock at sunset, his hand reached for the reel that was no longer there, and the empty feeling surprised him. The knife in his pocket could not cast a line. It could not bring back the sound of his grandfather’s laugh.
The next day, Eli found Marcus. “Any chance you’d trade back?” he asked, holding out the knife. Marcus shrugged. “Sure. I kind of missed the reel anyway.”

Walking home with the scratched old reel in his hand, Eli understood something he hadn’t before. The knife had been worth more in his imagination than in his pocket. The reel was worth more than it looked, because of everything it carried.

passages.title: The Library of Alexandria
paragraphs: More than two thousand years ago, in the Egyptian city of Alexandria, scholars set out to do something astonishing: gather all the knowledge in the world under one roof.

The Library of Alexandria became the greatest center of learning in the ancient world. It is said to have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls — the books of that time — on subjects from mathematics and astronomy to medicine and poetry.

The library was more than a storehouse. Scholars from many lands came to study, argue, and make discoveries there. Some of the ideas worked out in Alexandria, such as an early measurement of the size of the Earth, were remarkably accurate.
To fill its shelves, the city went to great lengths. Officials are said to have searched ships that docked in the harbor, borrowing any books on board so that copies could be made for the collection.
Over the centuries, the library declined. Through a mix of fire, war, and neglect, its scrolls were lost, and much of the knowledge they held vanished with them.

Today no one knows exactly how much was lost. The Library of Alexandria survives as a powerful symbol — a reminder of how much a society can gain by gathering knowledge, and how much it can lose when that knowledge disappears.

passages.title: The Choice
paragraphs: Tomas saw it happen. During the math test, his best friend Liam slid his phone halfway out of his pocket, glanced at the screen, and slid it back. Cheating.
Afterward, Liam was thrilled. “I think I aced it,” he said, bumping Tomas’s shoulder as they walked out. Tomas managed a weak smile.

That night, the weak smile would not leave Tomas alone. Liam was his oldest friend. They had built forts together and learned to ride bikes together. Telling on him felt impossible. But every time Tomas closed his eyes, he saw that phone sliding out, and something in his chest tightened.
The next morning, Tomas found Liam by the lockers. He did not go to the teacher. Instead, he said quietly, “I saw your phone yesterday. During the test.”
Liam’s face went red, then angry, then — slowly — ashamed. For a long moment neither of them spoke.
“I knew it was wrong while I was doing it,” Liam finally said. “I just… panicked.” He let out a breath. “I’m going to tell Mr. Reyes I want to retake it. The honest way.”
Tomas felt the tightness in his chest finally loosen. He hadn’t had to choose between his friend and the truth after all. By being honest with Liam, he had given Liam the chance to be honest too.

passages.title: The Dust Bowl: When the Land Blew Away
paragraphs: During the 1930s, a disaster struck the Great Plains of the United States. The land itself seemed to rise into the air, carried off in towering storms of dust. People called the region the Dust Bowl.

The trouble had several causes. For years, farmers had plowed up the wild prairie grasses to plant wheat. Those grasses had deep roots that held the soil in place. Once they were gone, nothing anchored the dirt.
Then came a long, severe drought. Without rain, crops withered and the bare soil dried into powder. When strong winds swept across the open plains, they lifted that loose soil into enormous clouds.

These storms, sometimes called “black blizzards,” could turn day into night. Dust crept into homes, food, and lungs. Many families lost everything, and thousands packed up and left, traveling west to look for work.

The disaster forced people to rethink how they treated the land. New methods were taught: planting trees to block the wind, plowing in patterns that held water, and letting fields rest. These practices helped the soil recover.
The Dust Bowl is remembered as a hard lesson. It showed that even something as vast as the land can be harmed by the way people use it, and that careful choices are needed to protect it.

passages.title: Moving Day
paragraphs: The moving truck swallowed the last box, and suddenly the house Mia had lived in her whole life was empty. Her footsteps echoed in rooms that no longer felt like hers.
She stood in her old bedroom, now just four blank walls and a square of brighter paint where her mirror had hung. “It doesn’t even look like my room anymore,” she whispered.
Her mother appeared in the doorway. “It isn’t,” she said gently. “A room is just a box. You’re taking the important parts with you.”
Mia didn’t believe her. On the long drive, she watched her town shrink in the side mirror until it disappeared, and the ache in her stomach grew with every mile.

But the new house was not as empty as she feared. As she unpacked, here was the chip in her favorite mug, there was the blanket that still smelled like home, and there, taped inside a box, was a note from her old neighbor: “Come visit. The treehouse will wait.”

That night, lying in her familiar bed in an unfamiliar room, Mia realized her mother had been half right. The house was just a box. But the home — the people, the memories, the small worn things she loved — had traveled with her after all.
It would take time to fill these new walls with that same feeling. But for the first time since the truck pulled away, Mia believed that she could.
